voice.instructions: Voice: a deep, resonant, warm male documentary narrator. Tone: quiet awe and gravitas, intimate rather than loud, like a premium nature documentary. Pacing: measured and unhurried, with natural pauses at commas and a short dramatic pause before each reveal. Emphasis: lean into vivid words (breathes, hidden, backwards, flood). Never sound like an advertisement.

intro: Seven hundred and forty-seven kilometres above us, a new kind of eye is circling the Earth.
This is NISAR, a radar satellite built by NASA and India's space agency. Every twelve days it maps almost all of the planet's land and ice, through cloud, by day and by night.
Today it is watching one place. Tonle Sap, in Cambodia. A lake that breathes.
pulse: It is monsoon season. For months, thick cloud hides this landscape from ordinary satellites.
But NISAR brings its own light: microwaves, twenty-four centimetres long, that pass straight through cloud. Press and hold to send a pulse.
pulse-done: That is radar. Calm water reflects the pulse away, so it looks dark. Stone and buildings throw it straight back, so they shine.
find: Somewhere below lies Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on Earth.
Its moat is almost two hundred metres wide: a perfect dark rectangle to a radar. Can you find it?
find-done: There it is. Nine hundred years old, and still echoing back to orbit.
The giant dark rectangle beside it is the West Baray, a reservoir dug by hand about a thousand years ago.
breath: Now watch a whole season, one satellite pass at a time.
Each monsoon the Mekong rises so high that the Tonle Sap river turns around, and flows backwards into the lake.
breath-done: Peak flood. Everything glowing was dry land in June.
The ground here is almost flat, so a few metres of rising water spreads across kilometres.
canopy: From above, a camera sees only green forest. But much of this forest is standing in water.
Long radar waves slip between the leaves, bounce off the water, then off the trunks, straight back to the satellite. Move the lens over the forest.
canopy-done: Hidden water, found. This drowned forest is the lake's nursery, where fish spawn among the flooded trees.
explore: This flood pulse feeds one of the richest inland fisheries on Earth. Dams and drought upstream are changing its rhythm.
With NISAR passing every twelve days, through any weather, that rhythm can be measured, season after season. Now explore it yourself.
